title: Understanding the Interplay between Memorization and Learning in Large Language Models
claim: A string is memorized once its training loss falls below the lowest loss it would reach from learning the language alone.
layout: 1 panel line plot; dotted-vs-solid curves, red threshold lines, double-arrow gap annotation
description: A single line chart with epoch (1 to 50) on the x-axis and loss (0 to about 1.7) on the y-axis. A legend at top left labels the blue curve s2. The solid blue curve is the training loss. It drops steeply, then decays to near zero. The dotted blue curve is the contextual loss. It falls to about 0.45 near epoch 6, then rises to about 1.1. Light blue shaded bands show variability around each curve. A red dash-dot horizontal line marks the minimum contextual loss, at about 0.45. A red dotted vertical line at epoch 6 marks where training loss crosses below it. A grey double-headed arrow near epoch 37 is labeled 'Contextual memorization'. It spans the gap between the horizontal red line and the solid curve. The eye goes first to the diverging curves and the red crosshair.
caption: Contextual Memorization. The solid curve is the training loss and the dotted curve is the contextual loss of a string $ s $, when it is inside and outside the training dataset $ D \sim L $, respectively (details in Section [ref]). Contextual memorization begins when training loss drops below the lowest contextual loss, i.e., the LLM generates $ s $ better than it would from learning the underlying language.
abstract: We investigate foundational questions about the interplay between memorization and learning in large language models (LLMs). When an LLM generates a string, can we disentangle the roles of rote memorization and contextual learning? Rote memorization results in an LLM regurgitating specific details of a training string, while contextual learning leads to the generation of new strings that follow generalizable patterns of the underlying language. Related questions of interest include: can an LLM avoid memorization when optimally learning a language?, and if not, can we design training schemes to reduce memorization and improve learning? To address these questions, we propose contextual memorization, a new measure that precisely disentangles memorization from learning. Using this measure, we establish that different training strings are memorized at different epochs in training, and that memorization of some training strings is unavoidable when optimally learning a language. Finally, we propose memorization-aware training, a scheme that dynamically down-samples training strings based on their memorization, and in doing so, equalizes learning across strings, reduces memorization, and improves learning. Our conclusions are supported by extensive experiments on multiple LLMs using formal languages as a controlled testbed, enabling precise language specification, exact string sampling, and elimination of data contamination; and further validated on natural languages.
